newsitem.title: USA: Senate Republicans press ahead with Louisiana probe.
newsitem.headline: Senate Republicans press ahead with Louisiana probe.

text.p: Senate Republicans decided Thursday to extend indefinitely a controversial probe of alleged fraud in Louisiana's 1996 Senate race over vehement opposition of Democrats who called it a witchhunt and farce.

The Senate Rules Committee on a series of straight party line votes decided to proceed with the investigation into whether Democratic Sen. Mary Landrieu's thin 5,788-vote victory arose from fraud or serious irregularites.

The Rules Committee vote on an open-ended probe followed the collapse of bipartisan negotiations aimed at wrapping up the probe in September or October. Democrats have threatened to slow down Senate business when they return from their August recess if the investigation is not completed swiftly.

Committee Chairman Sen. John Warner, a Virginia Republican, has acknowledged publicly that months of investigation have not substantiated the allegations made by Louis "Woody" Jenkins, the Republican Landrieu defeated.
But Warner said more questions have to be explored before the controversy can be laid to rest.
"There is no doubt this investigation is incomplete," said Warner, who won Republican support for his plan to draw from a $450,000 committee fund for campaign finance investigations.
Tempers flared at a vituperative committee hearing, a contrast after two days of unusual bipartisan harmony as Congress passed the balanced budget and tax cut bills.

"They'll rue the day they did this," said Sen. Wendell Ford of Kentucky, the senior Democrat on the Rules Committee. He said that if Republicans unilaterally issued subpoenas without Democratic agreement they would be breaking two centuries of precedent of protecting minority rights in committee.

"I don't remember this committee ever going on this kind of witchhunt," said Sen. Robert Byrd, a Democrat from West Virginia, saying that although the investigation had uncovered seamy things in Louisiana "there hasn't been a glove laid on Mary Landrieu so why do we continue this farce."
Jenkins lawyer Mark Seifert hailed the Rules vote as "a great day for the people of Louisiana."

"We are confident that the Republicans will conduct a full, fair and nonpartisan investigation that will let the chips fall where they may. Once and for all the people of Louisiana will know the truth," Seifert said.
